title: Bernard Stiegler
keyWorks: Taking Care of Youth and the Generations (2008)
What Makes Life Worth Living: On Pharmacology (2010)
summary: Bernard Stiegler (1952–2020) was a French philosopher of technology and a student of Jacques Derrida. He held that human beings have lived through technics from the very beginning: tools, writing and media are our external memory. In Symbolic Misery and Taking Care of Youth and the Generations he showed how the attention industry and marketing reshape our feelings and desires, and he looked for ways to take back care of them.
onEmotions: Stiegler’s key concept is the pharmakon: a Greek word that means both poison and remedy. Any technology — writing, a smartphone, a news feed, a substance — can both nourish our lives and destroy them; it all depends on how we handle it. Stiegler distinguished “desire,” which is tenderly attached to something singular and knows how to wait, from “drive,” which is short-lived and demands immediate satisfaction. The modern “attention economy” and hyperconsumption, in his view, turn desire into drive and take away our ability to feel and choose for ourselves — this is what he called “the proletarianization of sensibility.” So many painful states are not only a personal problem but also a consequence of our environment; and that means caring for yourself can take the form of learning anew how to live with your pharmaka.

anxiety.text: In 2016 Stiegler published The Age of Disruption, whose French subtitle asks: “How not to go mad?” It is about a world that changes faster than we can get used to it — and the anxiety you are carrying right now is largely about the same thing. Stiegler called our era a time of “disruption”: technologies are updated so rapidly that society, culture and the individual simply can’t develop ways of living with them. He considered this “maladjustment” between technology and life one of the main causes of today’s unease. Your anxiety isn’t only a personal weakness but also a response to a real break in rhythms. That doesn’t make it lighter, but it can lift some of the guilt: you’re anxious not because something is wrong with you, but because time really has fallen out of step.
anxiety.practice: Find one rhythm in your day that doesn’t speed up: making tea, watering a plant, walking a familiar route. Do it today twice as slowly as usual, as if time were back in step with you.

fear.text: “Epimetheus forgot about humans” — Stiegler opens Technics and Time with this myth. Handing out claws, fur and speed to the animals, the Titan left nothing for people. Your fear may be speaking the language of that same ancient feeling: as if you had nothing to defend yourself with. The human being was born “without qualities,” vulnerable, and so had to rely on fire and crafts — that is, on technics. For Stiegler this original lack isn’t a disgrace but the very essence of being human: we never stand on our own strength alone, but on supports we create and pass on to each other. Fear reminds you of your vulnerability. But it also points to a way out: not becoming invulnerable, but finding something to lean on — people, knowledge, reliable familiar practices.
fear.practice: Hold a familiar object in your palm — a key, a pen, a mug — and feel its weight. Say to yourself: “I don’t stand on my own alone” — and name one person you can lean on.

sadness.text: What makes life worth living? Stiegler put this question in the title of a 2010 book. The sadness you feel right now often answers it in reverse: something important to you has gone far away or out of reach. Stiegler believed that life is valuable because of our attachments — to people, activities, places and things we love and care for. Sadness often appears when such attachments weaken or break. It isn’t a malfunction but a sign that your capacity to cherish is alive. Stiegler stressed that true desire is always directed at something singular, irreplaceable, and he considered caring for such attachments the main work of life. Sadness shows you where that care is most needed right now.
sadness.practice: Touch one thing that connects you with what you are sad about — a cup, a letter, a plant. Do one small act of care for it: wipe it, water it, put it where you can see it.

grief.text: A voice on an old answering machine, handwriting on a postcard, a cup with a chipped handle: for Stiegler these aren’t trifles but memory living outside the head. In grief such traces suddenly become almost unbearably precious, because this is love that has lost its addressee. Stiegler called everything that holds experience outside us “tertiary retentions”: letters, photographs, voice recordings, objects, habits passed on to others. Thanks to them the past keeps talking to us. The person who has died hasn’t vanished without a trace: they remain in the memory inscribed in the world — in words you picked up from them, in things they touched. These traces can hurt, but they are also a way of continuing the bond. Handling them with care doesn’t mean getting stuck in the past; it means caring for what was precious.
grief.practice: Take in your hands one thing that holds this person, and tell out loud — to them or to yourself — one story connected with it. That way the trace becomes living memory again.

loneliness.text: How does one become oneself? Following Gilbert Simondon, Stiegler answered: only together with others. “Psychic individuation,” the becoming of an “I,” is inseparable from “collective individuation,” the becoming of a “we.” That is why loneliness hurts so sharply: the bond through which you become yourself is torn. We grow by sharing language, songs, work, common meanings. Stiegler was troubled that today’s media environment replaces this kind of communion with a stream: we see thousands of people but rarely do anything together with them. He called this the loss of the “we.” Your loneliness isn’t proof that something is wrong with you but part of a large problem of our era. And the way out isn’t in the number of contacts, but in doing something together, however small.
loneliness.practice: Suggest one small shared task to someone this week — cooking soup together, fixing a shelf, singing. Not “meeting up,” but doing something as two.

anger.text: What happens to a person who lacks the feeling that they exist? Stiegler asked this question again and again. Anger is one possible answer: it often flares up when something precious has been hurt. Stiegler believed that people need love of self in order to live — following psychoanalysis, he called it “primary narcissism” — that is, a basic sense that you matter and that your existence carries weight. When society and media turn people into interchangeable consumers, this foundation wears thin, and rage can build up in its place. This doesn’t justify destructive acts, but it explains where some of today’s anger comes from. You can treat your anger with curiosity: might it be telling you that you aren’t being seen or heard? Its energy can be turned toward caring for what truly matters to you.
anger.practice: Out loud, to no one in particular, say: “What matters to me is that…” — and finish the sentence. Listen to what kind of care your anger is really speaking about.

shame.text: In 1978 the twenty-six-year-old Bernard Stiegler ended up in a prison cell: he was convicted of armed robbery and spent five years behind bars. Many would hide such a past all their lives — shame makes us hide, and you probably know that feeling well right now. Stiegler didn’t hide this part of his life — later he spoke about it openly in his book Acting Out, describing how he began studying philosophy in his cell. For him prison became the place where he learned to read and think anew. From Stiegler’s point of view, a person isn’t a fixed essence but an “individuation,” an ongoing process of becoming. What you’re ashamed of is a moment in that process, not a final definition of you. You can acknowledge shame without making it your prison.
shame.practice: Read out loud one sentence that once helped you change — from a book, a song, someone’s letter. Let it remind you: you are a process, not a verdict.

guilt.text: Prendre soin — “to take care” — stands almost at the center of Stiegler’s philosophy. Your guilt speaks of responsibility: care is not an empty word for you. We live by caring for one another, for children, for the world, and this care can’t be handed over to a machine. In Taking Care of Youth and the Generations he wrote about the duty of the older toward the younger — to pass on attention, knowledge, the art of living. Guilt is often exactly the painful sense that care somewhere didn’t work out. You can take it not as a verdict but as a signpost: here is a place where it matters to you to care better. Stiegler spoke of care as a practice one learns all one’s life, and in any practice mistakes are inevitable. What matters is coming back to it.
guilt.practice: Make one small gesture of care toward whoever your guilt is about: a short message, a returned book, the question “how are you?” Not atonement — just coming back to the practice.

envy.text: Millions of people watch the same advertisement on the same evening — and by morning begin to want the same things. Stiegler called this the “synchronization of consciousnesses.” The envy squeezing you now may partly come from there: it seems others have something without which you are incomplete. So desire loses its singularity and turns into a race of comparisons. For Stiegler, genuine desire is always directed at something singular, while the industry offers interchangeable goods. Envy is partly an effect of the environment, not your personal flaw. Beneath it there may be a desire of your own, a real one, worth separating from the imposed one.
envy.practice: Imagine you have it — but no one, not a single person, will ever know. Stay with that picture for a minute: what is left of the desire?

emptiness.text: Symbolic Misery is the title Stiegler gave to a two-volume work of 2004–2005, about a society that has forgotten how to make its own meanings. The emptiness you feel, as if everything had lost its taste, may be part of that misery. It isn’t a lack of things, but a lack of the chance to take part yourself in making meanings — songs, images, stories, rituals. When we only consume what has been made for us, our sensibility, for Stiegler, is “proletarianized”: just as a worker on an assembly line loses their craft, a person in front of a screen gradually loses the ability to feel and express for themselves. Your emptiness may not be a personal inadequacy but a result of not having been allowed to be an author for a long time. Sometimes the first step is to make something of your own, however clumsy.
emptiness.practice: Make one small thing with your own hands — a doodle in the margin, a paper boat, a hummed tune. Not for the result, but to be an author for five minutes.

confusion.text: Savoir-faire and savoir-vivre — knowing how to do and knowing how to live, plus knowing how to think: Stiegler distinguished these three kinds of knowledge. A bewildered “I don’t know what to do” often means that at least one of them has been shaken. Stiegler believed that in an age of rapid technology all three quickly become outdated or are handed over to machines and algorithms, leaving people with the sense that they don’t understand the rules. It was this loss of knowledge that he called “proletarianization.” Your confusion isn’t stupidity but an honest reaction to a world where the old maps have stopped working. The way out, for Stiegler, is to learn anew little by little: patiently, together with others, at your own pace.
confusion.practice: Ask someone today to show you how they do one simple thing — making coffee, fixing a bike, keeping a budget. Watch how knowledge passes from hand to hand.

fatigue.text: The Romans called business negotium — literally “not-leisure”: work was defined by the absence of free time. The burnout you are in isn’t laziness but depletion, and Stiegler would probably see in it a lack of precisely that leisure. Stiegler recalled the ancient distinction between negotium — busy affairs, concern with profit — and otium — free time for reflection, friendship, art. He believed that today’s economy leaves almost no room for otium: even rest turns into consuming content, which also demands attention. Attention gets exhausted and has nowhere to recover. Burnout is both a personal misfortune and a symptom of how life as a whole is arranged. Rest that truly restores isn’t yet another series, but time when nobody wants anything from your attention.
fatigue.practice: Give yourself ten minutes of otium: no screen and no task. Look out the window at something slow — clouds, branches, passers-by.

boredom.text: Left with nothing to do, a child soon starts building a fort out of cushions: the psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott, on whom Stiegler drew, saw in this space of play the beginning of a world of one’s own. You are bored right now, and your hand reaches to fill the time with something at once. Stiegler would note that the entertainment industry is built so that boredom never gets a single second: the feed is always at hand. But, in his view, there is a price. Attention that is constantly captured from outside loses the ability to choose for itself what to rest on. Yet it is often out of a pause, out of “nothing is happening,” that your own interest is born. Boredom isn’t an emptiness to be plugged immediately, but perhaps a threshold beyond which your own desire might wake up.
boredom.practice: Sit in your boredom for five minutes without picking up your phone, like a child at a rainy window. Notice where your attention drifts on its own.

joy.text: In French an amateur is “one who loves”: Stiegler reminded us that the amateur does something out of love rather than for gain. Your joy seems to have something of this in it — the feeling that life is worth living. Music, a garden, books, a craft, friendship — everything into which long attention has been poured becomes a source of deep and inexhaustible joy. Stiegler distinguished it from the quick pleasure of consumption, which soon fades and demands the next dose. Your joy is precious, and it’s worth simply living it. And if you like, you can notice what it’s made of: perhaps there is something in it you have loved for a long time and that will go on gladdening you for a long time yet.
joy.practice: Spend five minutes with whatever brings this joy, like a true amateur: slowly, attentively, for its own sake — water the garden, play a tune, reread a favorite page.

love.text: Drive devours its object, desire cherishes it — Stiegler built his whole thinking about love on this distinction. Your tenderness is the heart of what he called desire. Drive wants to consume and forgets its object as soon as it is sated, while desire attaches itself to a singular, irreplaceable being and is never exhausted. For desire, the beloved doesn’t simply “exist” as a thing among things; in Stiegler’s phrase, they “consist” — they are held up by our faithfulness, attention and care. That is why love isn’t only a feeling but also a practice: it is sustained. This tenderness is one of the most precious and at the same time most fragile human capacities. It is worth caring for, like something alive.
love.practice: Give a person or creature you love one sign of attention that can’t be bought: a remembered detail, an unhurried question, a touch.

gratitude.text: The words you are thinking with right now weren’t invented by you: they were passed on to you by generations you never saw. Stiegler built a philosophy on this, and gratitude is the feeling in which it suddenly becomes visible — how much we have been given. Stiegler described the human being as a creature that inherits not only genes but a vast world created before it: language, tools, books, skills. He called this passing-on of experience through things and signs “epiphylogenesis” — the memory of the species written outside the body. Everything you can do, and the words you think with, were given to you by others. Gratitude is a very accurate feeling: it sees the real chain of generations on which each of us rests. And it gently invites the next step — to pass something on, and to become a link in that chain yourself.
gratitude.practice: Say thank you to one person who taught you something you still use — by phone, by message, in person. If that isn’t possible, show the skill to someone else.

hope.text: For the Greeks one word — pharmakon — meant both poison and remedy, and Stiegler made it the key to his whole philosophy. Hope, in this light, isn’t naivety but work. The technologies that today exhaust our attention could, in principle, also nourish it — it all depends on how we handle them and how we arrange life around them. Stiegler founded the association Ars Industrialis and proposed an “economy of contribution,” in which people don’t only consume but also create, share and learn. Hope is the knowledge that poison and remedy are made of the same substance. Nothing is finally doomed if it is cared for. Your hope is already the beginning of such care.
hope.practice: Choose one thing that is currently more of a poison for you — a habit, an app, a routine. Imagine the same thing as a remedy: what would have to change, just slightly?

nostalgia.text: A photo in an old album, a cassette, the smell of a school corridor: Stiegler held that a huge part of human memory is kept outside the head. Your nostalgia is a longing for a past that glows in such things. Stiegler distinguished what we perceive right now, what we remember, and “tertiary retentions” — recordings, photographs, songs that hold the past outside us. Listening to an old song, we live it anew each time, and a little differently: memory isn’t an archive but a living process. Nostalgia isn’t an escape from the present but a way the past goes on nourishing you. Stiegler might warn only against ready-made, factory-produced nostalgia, the kind sold through remakes and advertising. Your own nostalgia, though, can be a source: it holds what truly matters to you.
nostalgia.practice: Put on one song from that time and listen to all of it with your eyes closed. Then ask: what in it was most precious to me — and where is that in my life now?

craving.text: “Want it, got it”: Stiegler called this pattern a short circuit. When a sharp craving comes — for a cigarette, alcohol, your phone — it can be very strong, and there’s nothing to be ashamed of. Stiegler would call what pulls at us a pharmakon — a Greek word meaning both poison and remedy. Often a substance or a device really did once make life easier: it eased anxiety, gave you a breather. But Stiegler distinguished desire, which knows how to wait and builds long bonds, from drive, which demands immediate satisfaction. Hyperconsumption, in his view, trains us precisely in drives — in those very short circuits. A craving is a wave of drive: it rises and it falls. You can wait it out, asking what kind of self-care it is trying to stand in for.
craving.practice: When a craving comes, set a timer for five minutes and give your hands something slow to do: wash a cup, walk around the room. Keep asking yourself: what do I actually want — rest, comfort, company? Watch how the wave changes.

quote.text: The pharmakon is at once what enables care to be taken and that of which care must be taken.
quote.author: Bernard Stiegler
quote.source: What Makes Life Worth Living: On Pharmacology (2010)

addiction.text: Stiegler understood the word “pharmacology” more broadly than medicine: it is the art of living with what can be both poison and remedy. If you find yourself in the circle of addiction, it isn’t a moral failure. Stiegler described modern hyperconsumption as a system close to addiction: it cultivates drives in people that demand ever new doses — whether shopping, the feed or substances. Personal addiction, in this light, isn’t a strange deviation but the extreme point of where the environment keeps pushing. Every pharmakon calls for such a pharmacology. Such a practice is rarely built alone: for centuries it was kept by communities, rituals, traditions. The way out of the circle isn’t a heroic effort of will but the gradual building of new supports: people, habits, places where you are cared for.
addiction.practice: Name out loud one support that could help you in this circle: a person, a mutual-help group, a place. Promise nothing — just say its name.

hangover.text: What seemed like relief in the evening turns into poison by morning — Stiegler called this doubleness the pharmakon, and a hard morning shows it very vividly. Anxiety, shame and gaps in memory are added to the body’s wreckage. This isn’t a reason to punish yourself, just knowledge of how pharmaka work: they always have two sides. Stiegler insisted that the main thing in our relationship with any pharmakon isn’t shame but care — that is, attentive and patient treatment of yourself. Right now that care can be very simple. The morning after isn’t a verdict, but a time to look after your body and give yourself a little gentleness before sorting out yesterday.
hangover.practice: Open a window and stand by it for a couple of minutes, feeling the air on your face. Thoughts about yesterday can wait until your body feels better.

euphoria.text: A sparkler and a campfire burn differently, and Stiegler would probably ask which kind of fire this high will become. Right now everything seems possible. You can simply live this wave: it’s one of the strong human experiences. Stiegler would suggest noticing just one distinction — between what gives energy for a long time and what burns out quickly. He said that desire builds “long circuits” — bonds with people, work, plans — while drive lives by “short-circuiting.” Euphoria can become the start of something lasting: a meeting, an idea, a project. There’s no need either to distrust it or to try to stretch it out forever. Better to ask: what would this energy like to turn into once the wave recedes? Then the flash will leave behind not ash but a trace.
euphoria.practice: Write down on paper one idea that came on this wave, and put the note where you’ll see it tomorrow. In the morning, see what you want to keep.

crash.text: Advertising, premieres, celebrations — much of modern life, for Stiegler, is built as a series of flashes, each followed inevitably by a comedown. You seem to be in the second half of such a wave right now: the world looks faded. Such a comedown is familiar after a success, a bright evening, a long-awaited meeting, and it can be sharp. This is the rhythm of drive — a short surge and a fall. Desire, by contrast, for Stiegler, works over a long distance, and its rises are gentler but steadier. Your comedown isn’t proof that everything is bad, but the natural second half of the wave. Now is not the time to draw conclusions about your life. Better to take care of yourself and wait until the ordinary, unspectacular but reliable light of everyday life returns.
crash.practice: Go outside for five minutes and walk a familiar route, noticing ordinary things: signs, trees, other people’s windows. The dim light of everyday life is light too.

panic.text: “Support” is one of Stiegler’s most frequent words: a human being never stands on themselves alone. In panic you need support quite literally: your heart pounds, you seem not to get enough air, you feel you’re losing control — and it really is frightening. It can help to remember that a wave like this usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. Stiegler wrote a lot about how speed and a constant stream rob us of our own rhythm, and he believed people need simple, reliable supports that give that rhythm back. In panic you need the very first and simplest support — your body and what is right around you. There’s no need to understand or analyze anything right now. It’s enough to hold on to the present while the wave passes.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and hold the edge of a table or chair — that is your support. Find your rhythm: the exhale longer than the inhale, again and again, like a metronome, while the wave passes.

dread.text: “What’s the point of all this?” is a question Stiegler heard not only from individuals but from a whole era. When meanings suddenly seem hollow, existential dread arrives, and you seem to be in it right now. Stiegler wrote about a similar state as a malaise of the era, which he called “disbelief and discredit”: when people stop believing that their life and work mean anything, a deep unease spreads. He didn’t brush this feeling aside. But his answer was practical: meaning doesn’t lie ready-made somewhere outside — it is created by attachments and by care for people, work, the world. A person, for Stiegler, builds what makes their life worthwhile themselves, and does it together with others. Your question isn’t a verdict but the start of a search carried out in small steps.
dread.practice: Water a plant, feed the birds, help someone with a small thing — one little act of care. Let it be your answer to “what for” today.

fomo.text: Dozens of companies are competing for every second of your attention right now — Stiegler called this the “attention economy.” The fear of missing out, one of the most characteristic anxieties of our time, grows right out of it. It feels as if real life is happening without you. The feed is built so that it always seems something more important is happening somewhere else than where you are. For Stiegler, this destroys the very capacity for attention — long, focused, your own. Your fear is largely produced by the environment, not by some inadequacy of yours. The life you see on the screen has been selected and edited; the life you are living has not. Its value isn’t measured by how much it resembles the feed.
fomo.practice: Leave your phone in the room and spend five minutes by a window or in the yard. What is happening here, in your life, while the feed scrolls on without you?

sleepless.text: Not long ago the night switched the world off by itself: shops closed, broadcasts ended. Stiegler wrote that technology changes the very rhythms of our lives — and on a sleepless night you feel it especially: thoughts grow louder and time drags. The rhythm of sleep is also under pressure today: screens and feeds are available around the clock, and the line between day and night is blurring. This doesn’t mean your insomnia is “because of your phone”: it can have many causes. But it is a reminder that the night is time that belongs to you, not to the stream. Night thoughts are rarely accurate: you can write them down and set them aside until morning. You don’t have to demand that you fall asleep right away; you can gently give the night back its quiet.
sleepless.practice: If your thoughts won’t let go, write them down in pencil on paper, one line each, and tell yourself: “In the morning.” Then return to the feeling of the pillow and your breath.

betrayal.text: In the word “discredit” Stiegler heard the Latin credere, “to believe”: society, he held, rests on a credit of trust, on the belief that words mean something and promises are kept. Betrayal strikes exactly here, undermining trust not only in a person but in the world. When trust collapses, the ground disappears from under your feet. On a personal level betrayal feels similar: as if you no longer know what to believe. Your pain is proportionate to the loss: something truly important has been destroyed. But trust, for Stiegler, isn’t naivety; it is something created by care, and it can be created anew — with other people, slowly, on new foundations.
betrayal.practice: Get in touch with one person you still trust: a short call, a voice message. Notice what that trust rests on.

jealousy.text: A thing can be put in your pocket, a person cannot: Stiegler built his thinking about desire on this simple distinction. Jealousy is agonizing precisely because the fear of losing someone mixes with pain and anger — and with how much this person means to you. Stiegler distinguished the logic of desire from the logic of consumption. Consumption wants to possess: the thing must belong to me and be under control. Desire, in his view, is directed at the other as singular and irreplaceable — but also free. When anxiety takes over, love can quietly slide into the logic of possession, and then it hurts especially, because a person can’t be owned like a thing. There’s no need to shame yourself for jealousy; you can notice that behind it stands a desire that needs trust, not control.
jealousy.practice: Picture the person you love laughing among their own friends, without you. Stay with that picture for a minute and ask: what do I value in them if they don’t “belong” to me?

resentment.text: Memory, Stiegler said, is always selective: not a warehouse but a selection. An old grudge is exactly what memory has chosen and won’t let go of. Out of a huge stream we retain only a part, and what we retain largely determines who we become. A grudge is one of those retained things: by reliving it again and again, we make it part of ourselves. A grudge speaks not only of what was done to you, but also of how you are handling your memory now. This doesn’t mean “forgive and forget.” It means you can carefully choose what to give room to — and alongside the grudge, hold on to other things that are also true.
resentment.practice: Next to the memory of the hurt, call up another one — from the same time or something else entirely — that is also true but sounds different. Hold them side by side for a minute.

heartbreak.text: Messages kept for years, photos in the cloud, a profile that opens with one tap: Stiegler would call all this “tertiary retentions” — memory recorded outside us. When your heart is broken, these traces surround the pain on every side, and it already feels almost physical. They are a true pharmakon: they can comfort, and they can reopen the wound again and again. This doesn’t mean you need to delete them right away: the decision is yours and may come later. But it helps to notice at which moments they heal and at which they hurt. From Stiegler’s point of view, the love that was is real: it left a trace in who you have become. Grieving it is also a form of care for what was precious.
heartbreak.practice: Before you open the messages or photos, pause for one breath and ask yourself: will this be a remedy or a poison for me right now? Just notice the answer.

impostor.text: No amateur knows everything in advance — which is exactly why Stiegler valued that figure. If you are worn down by the feeling that you’re only pretending to know and soon it will come out, perhaps it isn’t only a personal fear. Stiegler wrote about the “proletarianization of knowledge”: in today’s world knowledge is increasingly stored in systems, algorithms and instructions, and an individual often feels they don’t really understand anything themselves. This feeling is very widespread, and it says a lot about the environment, not about your worth. The amateur learns out of love — and that is their strength. You’re not an impostor but a learner. Knowledge isn’t issued once and for all — it is constantly being won, and doubt is part of that path.
impostor.practice: Explain to someone — a friend, a colleague, or even the cat — one thing you know how to do and learned yourself. Notice how much knowledge you actually hold in your hands.

self_hatred.text: To Love, to Love Oneself, to Love Us — that is what Stiegler called one of his books, and love of oneself stands right in the middle of this chain, as a support for the rest. When it turns into hatred, one of the heaviest forms of pain arrives. The voice that condemns you is loud, but that doesn’t mean it’s right. Stiegler believed that every person needs love of self — following psychoanalysis, he called it “primary narcissism.” This isn’t vanity, but a basic sense that your existence has value and weight. Stiegler saw that today’s environment — comparisons, ratings, advertisements for perfect lives — constantly erodes this foundation. Your pain isn’t proof that you’re worthless but a sign that this foundation has been wounded. And what is wounded can be healed with care.
self_hatred.practice: Speak one sentence from your inner critic out loud — and then, in the voice you would use to comfort a friend, answer it the way someone who loves you would.

helplessness.text: Several years in a prison cell where others decide the routine — Stiegler knew powerlessness from the inside. Perhaps you know this torment right now too: seeing what is happening and not being able to change it. Later Stiegler said that it was in prison he began reading philosophy and turned his cell into a place of study: he couldn’t change his circumstances, but he could change his relationship to time and attention. He didn’t romanticize prison, but the experience convinced him that even in a very narrow space a tiny freedom remains — the freedom of attention. Your helplessness is real, but it doesn’t cancel everything. Somewhere nearby there is a small area in which you can still act.
helplessness.practice: Choose one object in the room and hold your attention on it for two minutes by your own will — that is the tiny freedom no one can take from you. Then do one small thing that is in your power.

procrastination.text: Thousands of engineers are working to make you open the feed right now instead of the document. So procrastination isn’t laziness. Stiegler would point out that our attention today is under constant attack: apps and feeds are designed to capture it, and they do so professionally. Fighting them with “willpower” alone is like arguing with an entire industry. Besides, tasks that require long attention — “long circuits,” as Stiegler would say — don’t give satisfaction right away, and the drive toward quick reward pulls you away. Procrastination isn’t your personal defect but a struggle for your own attention that everyone knows. What helps isn’t shame but gently adjusting your surroundings: the fewer lures nearby, the easier it is for your attention to return to the task.
procrastination.practice: Carry your phone into another room and take the very smallest first step of the task — open the file, take out the notebook. Just that.

uprooted.text: In your home town you knew where to get shoes mended and how to greet the neighbors — Stiegler would call this “knowing how to live.” After a move or emigration you lose not only a place but a whole environment in which you knew how to live. Drawing on Simondon, Stiegler distinguished an “associated” milieu, in which a person takes part, which they understand and can change, from a “dissociated” one, where they are only a consumer and an outsider. In a new place almost everything feels dissociated at first: you don’t know the rules and don’t take part in the life around you. Your sense of being lost is natural: it is the loss of that very knowledge, which was second nature in your old place. But an associated milieu can be built anew — through participation, small habits, people with whom you do things together.
uprooted.practice: Walk around your new neighborhood with no goal and find one place where you could not just be present but take part: a notice board, a workshop, a courtyard where people play chess.

overload.text: “Writing will weaken memory,” warns the Egyptian king in the myth Socrates retells in the Phaedrus. Following Derrida, Stiegler saw here the first pharmakon: writing weakens memory, yet without it there would be no philosophy. A head overfull with the feed, notifications and news, and yet strangely empty, is the same story in a new guise. Today the digital stream has become the pharmakon. It can expand the mind or exhaust it: when there is more information than attention can process, we learn not more but less. Overload isn’t a sign of your weakness but a natural reaction to a stream designed to capture attention. It needs boundaries — not a rejection of technology, but your own rhythm for dealing with it.
overload.practice: Turn off notifications in one app until evening. In the evening, notice what you actually missed.

quote.text: You have not discovered a potion for remembering, but for reminding.
quote.author: Plato

unreality.text: A concert watched through the screens of raised phones — Stiegler would probably recognize our time in that picture. The world seems to be behind glass and you yourself as if in a dream: this can be very unsettling, and Stiegler would offer only one angle, without claiming to explain it all. He wrote that more and more of our experience passes through screens and recordings: we see the world “as a broadcast,” and increasingly we turn our experiences straight into snapshots and posts. When perception is so heavily mediated, direct contact with things can weaken, and the world seems flat. Unreality may partly be a sign that your attention lacks the immediate. You can gently bring it back — through the body, through touch, through simple things done with your hands that no one needs to see.
unreality.practice: Touch something with a distinct texture — wood, fabric, cool water — and for a minute describe the sensation to yourself, without photographing anything.

awe.text: Justice can’t be put in a pocket, and beauty can’t be bought: Stiegler said such things don’t “exist” the way objects do, but “consist” — they are held up by our attention, faithfulness and care, and are therefore inexhaustible. Stars, mountains, music that take your breath away are a rare and precious encounter with them. That is what you are feeling now: something vast or beautiful that cannot be owned. Awe is a moment when we touch this inexhaustible. Stiegler contrasted such experiences with consumption, which quickly exhausts its object. Your wonder is one of the most living forms of desire. It doesn’t need to be explained or hastily captured. You can simply breathe it.
awe.practice: For one minute, look at what fills you with awe, without taking out your phone. Then close your eyes and rebuild it in memory — let it go on being held in you.

relief.text: Attention, for Stiegler, is usually stretched like a string: tasks, notifications and worries pull it in different directions. He saw attention as the most precious thing we have — and the thing someone is always trying to take from us. Relief is the long breath out after tension, and you can simply live it. In relief the string finally slackens, and you can see how much strength was going into holding on. It is a precious moment when your attention comes back to you. There’s no need to fill the freed-up space right away with a new feed or a new task. Stiegler valued otium — free time that belongs to no one and is filled with nothing. Relief is a good reason to give yourself a little of that time.
relief.practice: Without picking up your phone, sit for three minutes and notice where in your body you feel the relief. Let this time belong to no one.

calm.text: A child who has listened to a story all the way to the end is, for Stiegler, almost a model of how attention is born: slowly, in quiet. Your calm right now is of the same kind, and in a world where so much is built to excite and distract, it is rare. Stiegler considered attention one of the most important human values and stressed that it is formed slowly, in quiet and concentration. Calm is attention that nothing is disturbing and that isn’t hurrying anywhere. Your calm isn’t emptiness or idleness but the restoring of a capacity Stiegler saw as the basis of thought, care and love. You can simply enjoy it, without thinking about what to fill it with. Calm produces nothing, and that is its value.
calm.practice: Choose a sound you can hear right now, and for a minute simply listen to it, without judging or naming it.

inspiration.text: Being an author and not only a spectator is, for Stiegler, one of the most important human capacities. You seem to feel it from the inside right now: something wants to come into the world through you. It is a rare moment when you are not watching someone else’s work but making your own. Stiegler said that “symbolic misery” arises when people stop taking part in creating culture. Inspiration is the opposite of that misery: a moment when your sensibility becomes your own again. Stiegler valued amateurs — those who create out of love rather than for the market. Inspiration doesn’t have to be “professional” or useful. It is valuable as an act of taking part in the world. Best to catch it and start making while it’s still breathing.
inspiration.practice: Right now, sketch whatever came — messily, without editing, even on the back of a receipt. It’s a draft, not an exam.

schadenfreude.text: The feed works like a shop window, displaying other people’s successes and failures next to yours. Quiet joy at someone else’s failure comes to almost everyone, though few admit it. Stiegler didn’t write about it directly, but his analysis of the “attention economy” sheds a lot of light here. In his view, platforms turn life into a feed of comparisons, where another’s success feels like your own loss. Stiegler distinguished desire, which is directed at something of your own and knows how to wait, from drive — a short “here and now” impulse. Schadenfreude is a quick discharge of the drive to compare: for a moment it seems you’ve won. The feeling itself says nothing about what kind of person you are. But it can hint at where your own desire has been overshadowed by other people’s results.
schadenfreude.practice: Recall whose failure recently pleased you, and ask yourself under your breath: what do I want in this area — not in comparison, but for myself?

contempt.text: In States of Shock: Stupidity and Knowledge in the 21st Century (2012), Stiegler, following Deleuze, insists that stupidity, bêtise, isn’t a property of “others” but a possibility shared by everyone, philosophers included. The contempt you feel now is hard to admit, but it almost always has a reason: tiredness, disappointment, hurt at someone else’s carelessness. Knowledge, for Stiegler, is born precisely from the encounter with one’s own stupidity, not from superiority over someone else’s. Contempt is an attempt to move stupidity entirely outside, into another person, so as not to notice it in yourself. This isn’t a verdict on you: it’s simply easier that way. But if you see that the line runs through each of us, contempt can give way to something more alive — interest, argument, care for what hurt you.
contempt.practice: Think of a person you currently feel contempt for, and find in your memory one situation where you were even a little like them. Not for self-flagellation — just to soften the line.

disgust.text: The temperature in a room can be set with a remote — Stiegler held that our tastes are tuned from the outside today in much the same way. Disgust, a strong bodily “no” to a person, a situation, sometimes yourself, is unpleasant but informative. Stiegler wrote about “symbolic misery” — the impoverishment of our ability to feel and create meanings for ourselves when our tastes and desires are supplied by the marketing industry. He called this “aesthetic conditioning.” Disgust is a sign that your sensibility is alive and resisting: something in you refuses to accept just anything. Even disgust with yourself often speaks not of your being “spoiled,” but of a mismatch with an image imposed from outside. There’s no need to inflate disgust or be ashamed of it. You can question it: what exactly is it protecting you from, and what do you really value?
disgust.practice: Say out loud what you feel disgust toward right now, and finish the sentence: “What matters to me is that instead there would be…” Disgust often points to what is dear to you.

revenge.text: You were hit — hit back: Stiegler would call this reflex a “short circuit.” When you’ve been wounded, the wound demands an answer, and the wish for revenge says you were treated unjustly. A short circuit is a drive that demands immediate discharge. A long circuit is a path on which the impulse passes through time, words, other people and memory, and turns into something shared: a demand for justice, a story, a change in the rules. For Stiegler it is precisely such long circuits that make us human, and the industry of instant reactions keeps shortening them. The thirst for revenge is the raw energy of hurt. There’s no need to be ashamed of it, and no need to act on it by causing harm. It can be channeled into a long circuit: naming the injustice and seeking to have it acknowledged.
revenge.practice: Say out loud — to yourself or to someone you trust — in one or two sentences what exactly was unjust, without any plans for retaliation. That is how the impulse begins its long circuit.

anger_at_loved.text: Attention, Stiegler wrote in Taking Care of Youth and the Generations, is born not alone but between people — above all in the family and between generations. That is why it is so painful when it is the people closest to you that you snap at, and then feel ashamed; it happens very often, and it doesn’t cancel love. And today’s industry, in his view, hijacks attention: screens, notifications, endless urgency. When there’s no attention left, those close to us start to be felt as just one more demand among many. Anger is a signal of depleted attention, not proof that you’re a bad partner or parent. It’s no reason to take it out on anyone. But it is a reason to look after what your attention feeds on, and how.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger rises, ask yourself: how much attention do I have left right now, from 0 to 10? If it’s less than three, take five minutes of screen-free quiet before continuing the conversation.

ambivalence.text: The same medicine heals in a small dose and poisons in a large one — Stiegler built his concept of the pharmakon on this image. Loving someone and not being able to stand them is a very human mix, though frightening to admit. Stiegler applied the concept above all to technology, but the logic itself is broader: one and the same thing can both nourish and poison, depending on the measure and on how it is handled. A person close to you can be a pharmakon too: they give you support — and they also wear you out. Your ambivalence isn’t a mistake of feeling or a sign that the love is “not real.” It is an honest perception of complexity. Stiegler understood care as the art of handling a pharmakon: not rejecting it entirely and not taking it without measure, but looking for a form in which there is more remedy than poison.
ambivalence.practice: Open both palms. On one, place in your mind what this person gives you; on the other, what in you gets tired of them — one word each. Hold them like that for a minute and don’t choose.

guilty_relief.text: Sleepless nights, a phone you can’t switch off, constant readiness — Stiegler wrote that care, soin, can exhaust the one who cares. When a departure, a breakup or a loved one’s long illness is behind you, relief can be mixed with shame: how can you feel lightness if you love? But one doesn’t cancel the other. Stiegler wrote a great deal about care as the central human practice: caring for children, for memory, for the world, for oneself. Long strain settles into the body. When it ends, the body lets go. Relief isn’t a betrayal of love but the natural response of someone who has carried a weight for a long time. Love and relief can live side by side, and you can allow yourself both.
guilty_relief.practice: Say to yourself slowly, like a formula: “The love was there and still is — and I feel lighter. Both are true.” Repeat it three times, each time on the out-breath.

indifference.text: Désaffecté is what the French call an abandoned building, and it is what Stiegler, in Disbelief and Discredit, called people from whom industrial culture takes away the capacity to be affected: the word also means “deprived of affect.” Sometimes, where you “ought” to be moved — someone else’s grief, an important event, even your own celebration — there is silence inside, and that is frightening. The stream of images, news and stimuli is so dense that sensibility protects itself by going numb. This is part of what Stiegler called “symbolic misery.” Your indifference isn’t coldness of character but perhaps the fatigue of a sensibility overloaded beyond measure. It doesn’t mean you truly don’t care. Feeling often comes back not on command, but when it is given time and quiet.
indifference.practice: Choose one impression from today — a sound, a face, a taste — and stay with it for a minute without your phone. Notice whether anything inside responds, even faintly.

escape.text: Otium — free time for thought, creativity and care of oneself — Stiegler considered one of the first losses of our era. The urge to drop everything — your job, your city, your familiar role — can be sudden and very strong. This isn’t about leaving life, but about the wish to live differently. Stiegler described “proletarianization” — not only poverty, but the loss of your own knowledge, when work comes down to carrying out someone else’s procedures and leisure to consuming ready-made things. Even otium, in his view, is turned by modern industry into a commodity. The wish to escape is a longing for otium, for time that would be yours again. You don’t have to change your circumstances right away. You can start with a question: where do I still have even a little time of my own — and what is taking it away?
escape.practice: Go out for a five-minute walk without your phone — let it be a small piece of otium that belongs to no one. On the way, ask yourself: what exactly do I want to escape from, and what am I missing?

forbidden_attraction.text: “The wrong person” — and yet the pull is there. Stiegler, a very careful reader of Freud, would be in no hurry to pass judgment on an attraction like this, which comes uninvited and is unsettling. This feeling speaks of a living desire, not of your being corrupt. Following Freud, Stiegler distinguished drive from desire. Drive seeks immediate satisfaction. Desire is attached to something singular, unrepeatable, and is capable of sublimation — Freud’s word for turning the energy of drive into creativity, friendship, thought, work. Stiegler considered this capacity precious and saw how a culture of instant consumption erodes it. Such an attraction points to something you need to touch: aliveness, recognition, another version of yourself. There’s no need to decide anything right now — in either direction. You can simply ask yourself what this desire is about — it may tell you more than it seems.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Name to yourself in one to three words what this attraction promises you: aliveness? recognition? another version of yourself? Then look around: where else in your life does that promise sound?

social_anxiety.text: Likes, views, ratings: Stiegler warned that platforms turn life among people into constant counting. No wonder your throat tightens and you want to hide at the thought of being judged; behind this is a sensitivity to how you are seen. Stiegler described the human being through “individuation” — an ongoing becoming-oneself that happens not alone but together with others; he called it “psychic and collective individuation.” That’s why the gaze of others means so much to us. But platforms turn this togetherness into that very counting. Evaluation becomes the background of your whole life, and even a live conversation starts to feel like a test. Your anxiety isn’t only a personal trait but also a reaction to an environment where we are continuously measured. Real contact isn’t an exam but a shared becoming, in which you have a voice too.
social_anxiety.practice: Spend five minutes with someone around whom you are listened to rather than judged — in person or on the phone. Notice what is different about that conversation.

uncertainty.text: Devenir and avenir — “becoming” and “the future”: in French they sound almost the same, but Stiegler set them firmly apart. Right now it’s unclear to you what will happen, it’s hard to make plans, and your body lives in tension. Becoming is what simply happens on its own; the future is what people desire, imagine and create together. Stiegler believed that an era of rapid technological change floods us with becoming, leaving almost no room for the future: everything changes, yet it seems we choose nothing. Uncertainty isn’t only an anxious fog but also a space in which the future hasn’t yet been taken. You don’t have to know what will happen. You can ask yourself what small step today would make the future a little more yours, rather than something that merely happened.
uncertainty.practice: Take one small step today without waiting for clarity: make a call, find something out, clear a spot on your desk for a future task. Let it be a piece of avenir, not just devenir.

waiting.text: Différance — for Derrida, Stiegler’s teacher, deferral is woven into the very fabric of meaning. Waiting for an answer, for results, for news is exhausting: time drags, and there’s almost nothing you can do. Stiegler didn’t romanticize such torment at all, but he valued the very human capacity to wait. For him it is precisely what distinguishes desire from drive: drive demands “right now,” while desire knows how to defer and hold out through the interval. And today’s industry, according to Stiegler, trains us in instantaneity: notifications, one-hour delivery, the endlessly refreshing feed. That’s why waiting is especially hard to bear today — we’ve been trained out of it. Your restlessness is understandable, and the ability to dwell in the interval can be recovered little by little. Waiting isn’t empty time: in it you can care for what is within your reach now.
waiting.practice: Choose one small task that can be finished while you wait — and do it slowly, without checking your phone.

regret.text: Reread an old diary and it reads a little differently each time — for Stiegler, that is how memory works. Regret that keeps coming back shows that the past matters to you. Stiegler thought a great deal about memory and singled out a special kind — “tertiary retentions”: memory carried outside us, into recordings, photos, letters, diaries. His important idea: the past doesn’t lie still. Each time we return to it, we select and interpret it anew — and by that selection we are already choosing what our future will be. A person, for Stiegler, is an unfinished “individuation,” a process rather than a final result. Your regret isn’t a verdict but material: you can build your next step from it. The past can’t be changed, but you can change how it works in you — what lessons you choose from it and what you decide to carry forward.
regret.practice: Write down what you regret, and below it what this experience showed about your values. This isn’t an excuse, but a different reading of the same story.

longing.text: The irreplaceable is one of Stiegler’s key words: desire, in his view, is always directed at what cannot be replaced. That is why your longing is so precise: you don’t need “someone,” you need exactly this person. Consumer culture teaches the opposite, interchangeability: everything can be upgraded, a substitute found, scrolled past. Your longing is a quiet resistance to that logic. It testifies that the capacity for what Stiegler called desire in the proper sense — attachment to the unrepeatable — is alive in you. Longing hurts, and there’s no need to prettify that. But it is a form of faithfulness to what was dear to you. In time it can become a memory that not only wounds but also warms.
longing.practice: Name under your breath three things that were unrepeatable about this particular person: a gesture, a pet phrase, a laugh. Let yourself feel gratitude for them, even if the sadness remains.

world_pain.text: Entropy is the measure of decay, and Stiegler called our time the “Entropocene”: an era when humanity is exhausting its resources, including its inner ones. Pain for the wars, disasters and injustice the news reports every day is heavy, and there is nothing excessive about it. In his late works Stiegler wrote about an era of “disruption” — rapid ruptures that neither laws, nor feelings, nor thought can keep up with. A nonstop stream of alarming news, in his view, overloads attention and leaves a person powerless before the scale of what is happening. But Stiegler also looked for an answer — “negentropy”: local actions that create order, meaning and care in the face of decay. You don’t have to carry the whole world alone. Your pain is a sign that you care, and it can be turned into small acts of care close to you.
world_pain.practice: Do one small act of negentropy today — help a neighbor, tidy a patch of the yard, say a kind word to someone. And give yourself an hour without news.

rejection.text: To Love, to Love Oneself, to Love Us — in the title of this 2003 book Stiegler built a chain in which love of oneself links love of another and love of “us.” Being turned away strikes at this chain: as if you’d been told there is no place for you. There Stiegler wrote that life requires “primary narcissism” — a healthy, basic love of self, without which it is impossible to love others. This love isn’t born in isolation: it grows out of how we are accepted, listened to, reflected back. But Stiegler has another idea too: individuation, our becoming ourselves, runs through many bonds, not through one. Rejection by one person or one group is the breaking of one thread, not a verdict on the whole fabric. Your pain is real. And at the same time it doesn’t define your worth.
rejection.practice: Walk in your mind through your fabric of connections — people, activities, places — and name at least five threads. Notice: one has broken, but the fabric is wider.

abandonment.text: A teddy bear, the corner of a blanket — Donald Winnicott called them “transitional objects,” and Stiegler saw in them the first supports a person finds outside themselves. The fear of being abandoned has its roots in the same place, at the very beginning of life, when we depend entirely on others. Stiegler considered this dependence not a weakness but the essence of being human. A person is born helpless and becomes themselves only thanks to care: adults pass on language, memory and skills. Winnicott showed how, with the help of such an object, a child learns to bear the mother’s absence. The fear of being left without support is an echo of that original dependence, not a sign that you are “too much.” In adult life, too, supports can be multiplied: people, activities, places and habits that hold you when any one person drifts away.
abandonment.practice: Recall your adult “transitional object” — a thing, place or ritual that calms you. Turn to it today, deliberately and gently.

unrequited.text: Consister — “to consist,” “to hold together”: Stiegler used this verb for what never exists as a thing and yet holds us. Love without an answer hurts doubly — the feeling is there, but no answer comes — and it can’t be called foolishness. Stiegler distinguished what “exists” from what “consists”. The objects of our deep desire — love, justice, beauty — never fully exist as things that can be obtained, but they “consist”: they act in us, guide us and hold us. Your love is real even if it has met no answer: it has already changed you, taught you attention and tenderness. Stiegler considered the capacity for such desire precious, especially in a world where everything comes down to quick acquisition. There’s no need to rush the pain. In time, what you discovered in yourself may find a new addressee.
unrequited.practice: Write down what this love has taught you — what tenderness, what kind of attention. That remains yours, regardless of the answer.

humiliation.text: A voice that counts for something in the shared world of words, images and meanings was, for Stiegler, as much a need as food and safety. Humiliation strikes exactly at it: as if you’d been stripped of your dignity in front of others. Being deprived of such a voice Stiegler called “symbolic misery.” Humiliation works in a similar way: it tries to push you out of the circle of those whose voice counts. Stiegler insisted that the symbolic world doesn’t belong only to the powerful: it is made by everyone who speaks, writes, remembers, tells stories. Humiliation speaks of the actions of those who humiliated you, not of your worth. What helps you reclaim your dignity is precisely speech: naming what happened in your own words and being heard by at least one person.
humiliation.practice: Tell one person you trust about what happened, calling things by their names. Let your voice be heard by at least one listener.

body_shame.text: Who decided what the “right” body should look like? Stiegler would give an unexpected answer: largely, the screen. If you are unhappy with your body right now, it isn’t your fault. Stiegler wrote about “temporal objects” — films, shows, videos that unfold in time and capture our consciousness while we watch them. The industry, in his view, “synchronizes” millions of consciousnesses: everyone watches the same thing at the same time and gradually begins to desire the same things. That is how a single image of the “right” body takes shape — selected, retouched, repeated thousands of times. We compare our living body with it, though no one has retouched ours. Your dissatisfaction is largely an echo of other people’s pictures, not the truth about you. The antidote is to reclaim your own perception: to notice what your body can do, feel and remember, not only how it looks.
body_shame.practice: Put your palm on the part of your body that worked especially hard today — legs, back, hands — and silently thank it for something specific. No judgments about appearance.

illness.text: Glasses, a cane, a notebook, other people’s helping hands — Stiegler called all this “prostheses” in the broad sense and held that human beings have never lived without them. When the body lets you down and the familiar sense that it simply “works” collapses, it’s frightening and exhausting. For Stiegler, leaning on them isn’t humiliating but human nature itself. Stiegler also drew on the philosopher of medicine Georges Canguilhem: health isn’t simply the absence of illness, but the capacity to create new norms of life, adapting to changed conditions. Illness doesn’t cancel you: it calls for inventing a new routine, new supports, a new measure of strength. This doesn’t have to be done heroically. Small steps and a willingness to accept help are enough.
illness.practice: Allow yourself to lean on one support a little more than usual today: ask for help with a small thing, reach for something comfortable, put off an unnecessary task.

pride.text: Stiegler began learning philosophy in a prison cell, from books and letters — he knew what it means to learn something by yourself. Pride in something you’ve done is a good feeling, and there’s no need to hide it out of modesty. Stiegler held the figure of the amateur in high regard — in French, amateur, from the word for “to love”: someone who does something out of love for it, not only for the result or the pay. So the moment when you yourself have created, mastered or finished something matters doubly for Stiegler: it is a reclaiming of knowledge and a step in your individuation — your becoming yourself. Pride is a sign that you took part in your own life rather than just consuming it. You can give it a place: without exaggerating or brushing it off, notice what you learned along the way.
pride.practice: Tell someone — or yourself, out loud — what exactly you did and what you learned along the way. Let yourself be glad, without brushing it off.

melancholy.text: We hear a melody as a whole only because we are still holding the notes that have sounded and already awaiting the next ones: Stiegler was very fond of this example from Edmund Husserl. Your quiet, almost tender sadness is like such a melody — sad but not heavy, and there’s no need to chase it away or cure it. Our consciousness works the same way: the present is always woven from echoes of the past and expectations of the future. Melancholy is a moment when these threads become audible: the past sounds within the present, like a fading melody. Your bright sadness is a sign of a deep, “long” time within you, so rarely available in the rush of modern life. Stiegler would call such a state the opposite of a “short circuit.” You can simply stay in it for a while.
melancholy.practice: Put on a melody that resonates with this mood and listen to it from beginning to end, without doing anything else at the same time.
